segments.narration: Pi shows up in a wave, in a probability curve, in the fabric of prime numbers — and yet none of those things look like a circle. What is this number, and why is it hiding everywhere?

Draw a circle with a marked point on its rim sitting on a horizontal line. Show the point touching the line, then the circle rolled one full turn, leaving a segment exactly one circumference long. Narrate: this distance is what π measures — how many diameters fit around the edge.

Set the diameter to exactly one unit. Watch where the circle's edge lands after one full roll — past three, past three point one, past three point one four — always stopping at the same irrational place, no matter how big or small the circle.

That ratio — circumference divided by diameter — is exactly what we call π. It is not a formula imposed on circles from outside; it is a fact every circle obeys, no matter its size. So we write it simply: C equals π times d.

Now let's see why the area of a circle is π r squared. Imagine slicing the circle into thin wedges and rearranging them — half pointing up, half pointing down — into a shape that looks more and more like a rectangle. Its width is half the circumference, which is π r, and its height is r. So area equals π r times r.

But here's an honest complication: π is irrational. No fraction ever equals it exactly. Twenty-two sevenths gets close, three-fifty-five over one-thirteen gets remarkably close, but every fraction lands just slightly off — the decimal of π never repeats, never terminates, forever.
And yet π shows up far beyond circles — in waves, in probability, in quantum mechanics. Wherever rotation, cycles, or round symmetry hide, π follows. It is, at its core, the geometry of turning.
